newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Court stays execution call for British nurses.
newsitem.headline: Court stays execution call for British nurses.

text.p: An Australian court on Friday temporarily barred the brother of murdered Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford from calling for the death penalty for two British nurses charged with killing her in Saudi Arabia.
The South Australian state Supreme Court ordered Frank Gilford not to make further comments on behalf of his family until his mother's mental state had been assessed.
Under Saudi law, a call for the death penalty by a victim's family must be unanimous, lawyers representing the British nurses told the court.
The lawyers said Yvonne's mother, Muriel Gilford, suffers from Alzheimer's disease and is not mentally competent to agree with her son's call for execution.
Judge Len King issued a temporary restraining order against Frank Gilford pending a study of his mother's mental state.

"Until further orders, the defendant (Frank Gilford) be restrained...from further advising the Saudi Arabian court that it is the unanimous view of the heirs that the death penalty be inflicted...," King said in his judgment.
King ordered Frank Gilford to notify the Saudi court of his ruling and that Muriel Gilford's health documents be made available to the British nurses' lawyers.

Yvonne Gilford, 51, was found murdered in her dormitory at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11 last year. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.
British nurses Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLaughlan, 31, have been charged with murdering Gilford, but have said they are innocent, despite initially signing confessions.
If found guilty the nurses face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally a public beheading by the sword.
King made the order after being told by the nurses' lawyers that the matter was urgent as the Saudi court could impose a verdict and sentence when it resumed on Sunday.

He said there was clear evidence Frank Gilford had told the Saudi court it was the unanimous view of the heirs that a death penalty should be imposed and that the consequences of a mistake in the matter could be dire and irreversible.
"There can be no doubt that those statements may operate to the serious detriment of (Parry and McLaughlan)," he said.
Dick Whitington, acting for Parry and McLaughlan, earlier told the court that there could be no execution if there was lack of unanimity among the heirs.
Whitington said Frank Gilford's statements representing his mother's view on the penalty were "knowingly false and malicious...(and) calculated to cause damage to (the British nurses)".

"At all material times (Muriel Gilford) has suffered from Alzheimer's disease and is mentally incompetent and is incapable of forming a view as to whether or not the death penalty should be inflicted...," the nurses said in their statement of claim.
Whitington said there had been seven hearings of the Saudi court to date with a further hearing scheduled for Sunday.
"This may be the final hearing and it may be that a verdict and sentence will be imposed on this date or shortly thereafter," he told the court.

Michael Boylan, acting for the Gilfords, who did not attend Friday's hearing, rejected the need for urgency, saying a sentence would not necessarily be handed down on Sunday and an appeal process could take "up to a couple of years".
"The South Australian proceedings are an attempt to delay or somehow interfere with the processes of law in Saudi Arabia," he said.
Outside the court, Boylan said the injunction was solely an interim measure to support the status quo, but he could not comment further until he had spoken to the Gilfords.

Frank Gilford could not be contacted and his wife, Laurel, speaking by telephone from the couple's home in the farming town of Jamestown, said they did not wish to comment until a verdict had been handed down by the Saudi court.
